entities.summary:
Columbia Pictures is one of Hollywood's major studios, founded in 1924 by Harry and Jack Cohn and Joe Brandt, and now owned by Sony Pictures Entertainment. Columbia's history spans the transition from silent films to talkies, through the Golden Age of Hollywood, to the modern blockbuster era — producing It Happened One Night (1934, first film to win all five major Oscars), Mr. Smith Goes to Washington (1939), From Here to Eternity (1953), The Bridge on the River Kwai (1957), Lawrence of Arabia (1962), Easy Rider (1969), Kramer vs. Kramer (1979), Gandhi (1982), and Men in Black (1997).

Harry Cohn ran Columbia as a dictator from 1924-1958, using information from a private detective agency against his staff, refusing to pay for proper production facilities, yet producing many of Hollywood's greatest films under director Frank Capra's partnership. Capra's Columbia films — It Happened One Night, Mr. Deeds Goes to Town, Mr. Smith Goes to Washington — defined the 'Capra-corn' genre of American populist optimism. The Cohn era ended with his 1958 death.

Sony Corporation acquired Columbia in 1989 for $3.4 billion — a Japanese conglomerate owning an American cultural icon that caused congressional debate about Japanese investment in American media. The Spider-Man franchise (2002-present) and the Jumanji franchise became major Sony-Columbia commercial successes. The film adaptation of the hit musical La La Land (2016) and the Academy Award-winning Marriage Story (2019) represent Columbia's continuing art-house prestige track.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Columbia Pictures produced Lawrence of Arabia, Easy Rider, Gandhi, and Spider-Man — spanning 100 years of cinema history — and its Sony acquisition became a landmark case in debates over foreign ownership of American cultural institutions.
